ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short-to-medium turns outside the presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is informal and overlap-prone, with quick greetings, technical check-ins, side comments, laughter-like reactions, and occasional false starts or repeated words. Speakers use frequent fillers and hedges—“um,” “yeah,” “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know”—especially when qualifying interpretations or asking questions. Formality shifts noticeably: introductions and presentations are professional but conversational, while transitions and discussion are casual and friendly. Questions are often prefaced with praise, self-deprecation (“quick,” “naive”), or framing language, then become exploratory and multipart. Participants generally build on one another’s points rather than challenge directly; disagreement or uncertainty is expressed indirectly through caveats, alternative explanations, and admissions of open questions. Responses tend to validate the question first, then think aloud through possibilities, with occasional interruptions, clarifications, and unfinished phrasing typical of live online discussion.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I wonder if it's even the same thing- like, are we measuring the same thing in both places?
  - Honestly no idea. Maybe? I'd have to look at how they set it up.
  - Huh. Okay, so what if we just asked them?
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Understanding why a low-cost point-of-care blood test is adopted in some rural clinics and left in a drawer in others.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Okafor
speakers.background: A biomedical engineer with 11 years of experience evaluating diagnostic devices in primary-care and rural settings. She has led field reliability assessments of battery-powered analyzers, including log-file review, environmental stress checks, consumable compatibility testing, calibration audits, and maintenance workflow analysis with local technicians.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats uneven uptake first as a system-performance question: a test cannot become routine if its power supply, storage conditions, consumables, calibration status, or repair pathway make results unreliable or burdensome. She will lead the technical review of device logs, battery charging conditions, storage temperatures, stock and expiry status, calibration records, and maintenance arrangements, while asking how those material conditions intersect with staff routines.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
speakers.background: A medical anthropologist and postdoctoral researcher with 4 years of fieldwork experience in rural health services, focused on diagnostic decision-making, professional hierarchies, and referral practices. He uses semi-structured interviews, shadowing, workflow observation, and comparison of formal protocols with everyday practice.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo approaches adoption as a social and organizational practice rather than a simple decision to use an available tool. He will examine how different cadres understand the test and its results, who is seen as authorized to request or run it, how patients and community health workers shape testing decisions, and how informal relationships influence referral. He is attentive to the possibility that routine use may depend on trust, role boundaries, and locally meaningful ideas of good care, though he is still working out how best to connect these observations to a device-focused evaluation.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Lillian Mensah
speakers.background: A public-health researcher with 14 years of experience studying district health systems, primary-care implementation, and diagnostic screening programs. She has worked with health authorities on service mapping, supply-chain assessments, referral pathway reviews, staffing analyses, and permissions for multi-clinic field studies; she is already liaising with the district health office for this project.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Lillian frames adoption as an implementation and health-system issue: a clinic's ability to use a test routinely depends on whether procurement and resupply work, program guidance is actionable, staff coverage permits testing, and referral pathways make same-day screening worthwhile. She will lead district approval and clinic-access coordination, then map procurement, resupply, screening guidance, formal referral pathways, staffing coverage, and relevant district-level arrangements. She expects the strongest explanation to emerge by comparing these system conditions with the engineering and ethnographic findings across all six clinics.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting involving all three disciplines. The biomedical engineer explains that the team needs to inspect device logs, battery charging conditions, storage temperatures, consumable stock, calibration records, and maintenance arrangements at each clinic. The anthropologist explains that interviews and observation should examine how staff interpret the test, who is authorized to order or run it, how patients and community health workers influence decisions, and how informal referral relationships operate. The public-health researcher explains that the study must map procurement and resupply, screening-program guidance, formal referral pathways, staffing coverage, and district-level permissions. The group must agree on a coordinated six-month next-step plan that assigns leads by discipline, identifies shared work and sequencing, and makes clinic participation and district approval explicit dependencies. The team should decide that public health will obtain district approval and coordinate clinic access first; engineering and anthropology will then conduct a joint orientation visit at each site, followed by discipline-led data collection with a shared site timeline; all three disciplines will jointly compare findings across the six clinics and develop explanations for routine use versus nonuse. No conflict or hidden issue needs to be introduced.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Hi, before we start—did the revised district approval form from last week ever come through to everyone? I may have missed it in the email thread. For today, I was hoping we could get clearer on what each of us needs to see at the clinics, so I can build that into the access request and put together a realistic shared, shared visit sequence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Sorry, was the clean version of the clinic-information sheet attached to that same thread? I saw the approval form, I think, but not the sheet. For access, I would need some ordinary observation time around triage and testing. And I am still unsure whether patient conversations will be permissible at every site. The staff-side question is partly who is understood to be allowed to decide that the test gets- who is understood to have the authority to decide that the test gets run.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Mm, yes, that's important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Did we ever confirm the analyzer model number in last week's equipment inventory? I need that before I fix the technical checklist, because the log download method may differ by model. And Lillian, could the access request ask clinics to have the device, the log-ins if there are any, calibration records, and unopened consumable boxes available when we arrive? I was going to say, for the- actually, that's what I need for the checklist.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did anyone ever get the revised inventory spreadsheet with the model field completed? I'll put those materials in the request, yes, though I'd rather phrase it as having them available if feasible, not as a compliance, compliance exercise. Amina, especially for the low-use sites, which supply and maintenance details would let us tell a short disruption from a more persistent readiness problem?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: For a short disruption, I'd need the delivery and expiry dates by lot, then the battery and log history around that period, to see whether the device was actually available and capable of running. For a persistent problem, stronger signals would be repeated stock gaps, overdue calibration, recurring fault codes, or an unresolved repair. Could procurement show when supplies physically reached each clinic, rather than just when the district dispatched them?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: I’ll ask for the delivery paperwork or receiving records at clinic level, if they exist, rather than treat the district dispatch date as arrival. That discrepancy between the two low-use clinics could be storage, informal redistribution, or simply that nobody was offering the test, so I think we need to trace the cartons and also, also ask what happened to demand once they arrived.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: One thing from last week, did the draft access request include community health workers or only clinic staff? If cartons are being redistributed, or if the test just isn't being offered, they may know how people are being directed before they get to triage. I wouldn't treat a device that's ready but unused as straightforwardly a demand issue. There may be this informal sense that somebody else has to authorize it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Did the revised inventory ever clarify whether the low-use clinic with the charged battery had any fault or error history? I agree, Mateo, readiness is necessary, but it clearly isn't sufficient. When staff get a result that doesn't fit what they see clinically, what do they usually do with it? Do they repeat it, send the patient on, or, um, stop using the analyzer?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the referral-flow diagram from last week ever get circulated? Because when a result conflicts with clinical judgment, I’d want to see if repeating it or referring anyway is formally expected, and then observe what actually happens. Those responses may be less about distrust of the analyzer itself and more about who feels able to take responsibility for the next step, or...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the district's current screening guidance ever get attached with the referral diagram? I need to check whether it says what should happen after a discordant result, because that may be a formal pathway problem rather than- it may not be an individual clinician deciding not to trust it. And Mateo, if we include CHWs in the access request, how would you introduce that without it sounding like we're asking them to account for staff practice?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the version of the access request with the CHW language come through after last week? I'd frame them as people who help us understand the care and referral pathway before clients arrive, not as witnesses to whether staff are following procedure. We could ask how clients are directed, what information travels with them, and when a same-day test is seen as relevant, without asking them to evaluate particular clinicians.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the clean clinic-information sheet ever get circulated? That framing feels much safer. I’ll include CHWs as people who can describe how clients move through screening and referral, including before they get to the clinic, rather than asking them to comment on anyone’s performance. And I’ll check with the district office whether they need separate permission or just a clinic-level introduction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the district office say if those introductions can go through the clinic in-charge, or do CHWs need to be approached through their own supervisor? It matters a little for the interviews because I don't want their participation to seem like an extension of clinic oversight. They may describe the referral pathway pretty differently if that distinction is clear.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the district liaison email ever specify the CHW reporting line? I don't think it did, so I shouldn't assume the clinic in-charge is the right route. I'll ask the district office whether introductions should come through the CHW supervisor, and whether they want a separate information sheet. That may also make it clearer that participation isn't part of the clinic performance— isn't part of clinic performance review.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Did the district guidance and referral diagram ever get sent together? I’m asking because, when we do get access, I’d like the first joint walk-through to follow the actual client path before I start pulling logs and records. That may show whether an apparently unused but technically ready analyzer is sitting outside the point where anyone is, is authorized or expected to order the test.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the latest clinic-site template get circulated, or is that still the older version? I like beginning with the client path, so if the joint orientation is after approval and introductions, we can walk from arrival through testing and referral before any of us go into separate records or interviews. I’ll make that common first step explicit in the access request, though the dates will have to wait on the district and clinic...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, that sequence matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the revised common template ever come through with a place for who initiates, runs, and, um, acts on the result? I think the walk-through should capture that separately at each handoff, because the device can be physically on the client path and still be socially outside anyone's remit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the revised template with those handoff fields ever get sent, or are we still working from the old one? That would be useful for the system map too, to show who is formally meant to initiate, run, and act on the result, and who actually does it. We should probably capture whether staffing coverage changes those handoffs by day or shift, because it could look like reluctance when really nobody is available.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the shift-roster extracts ever come through with the template? I'd include coverage, but when the person who's nominally responsible is absent- we'd also need to ask what happens then. Can somebody else run the test, or does it just wait? Because that's where an informal role boundary may become visible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the roster extract ever come through with the named cadre, not just the headcount? Because yes, I think we need to map the contingency, which shifts the test can actually be offered on, who can cover, and whether the referral destination is reachable that day. Otherwise a clinic may look low-use just because the pathway only exists intermittently.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the roster extract ever get resolved with the district? I’d be cautious about treating “coverage” as just a staffing variable. If a nurse is there but feels they can’t initiate or act on the result without the in-charge, that’s a different kind of interruption. Could the walk-through ask, very concretely, what happens to an eligible client on a day when that person is absent?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Did the updated site template ever come through with a field for where the analyzer is kept? And on the absent-person scenario, I would also ask whether the substitute is permitted and able to run the control or resolve an error code. A nominal cover arrangement may still leave the instrument effectively unavailable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Hm, yes, that is revealing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the current screening guidance ever come through in full, rather than just the excerpt? I think the absent-person scenario needs to sit alongside the formal rule. Who's permitted to test, who can act on a positive or discordant result, and whether a substitute can actually refer. Otherwise, we may call it a staffing issue- a staffing gap, when the clinic has staff but no workable authority chain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Did the final inventory file ever come through with the model numbers? The formal permissions and the practical authority chain, those need to be recorded alongside the technical checks. If the substitute cannot run controls, interpret an error, or access the consumables and charger, then for that shift the analyzer is not, not really available, regardless of what the roster says.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Did the revised access-request draft ever come back from the district liaison? I’ll add those practical authority and access points to the common template, who can reach the consumables, charger, controls, and make a referral on a given shift. But we should leave the visit dates open until approval and the clinics, clinics confirm. Then the joint walk-through can test whether the written pathway actually holds on an ordinary day.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Did the updated access-request draft ever get circulated after Lillian's edits? Sorry, I know we're over. Let's- let's leave the rest for the next meeting. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: All right. Goodbye, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lillian Mensah
transcript.text: Okay, speak soon.
